children.title: Paramount Settles Trump’s 60 Minutes Lawsuit for $16 Million
children.description_short: Paramount agreed to pay $16 million to settle Trump’s lawsuit over a 60 Minutes interview; the settlement did not establish that the interview was improperly edited.
children.description_medium: On July 2, 2025, Paramount agreed to pay $16 million to settle Donald Trump’s lawsuit over a 60 Minutes interview with Kamala Harris. PBS NewsHour reported that Trump alleged the interview was edited to improve how Harris sounded, which CBS denied. Paramount said the money would go to Trump’s future presidential library and that CBS would not issue an apology. PBS also reported that Paramount was seeking merger approval from the Trump administration; concerns about a connection were reported as allegations, not proven as an exchange.
children.description_long: On July 2, 2025, Paramount agreed to pay Donald Trump $16 million to settle his lawsuit over a 60 Minutes interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris. Trump alleged that the interview had been edited to improve how Harris sounded; CBS denied the allegation. Paramount said the payment would go to the president’s future library and that the settlement did not require an apology. The case therefore ended in a payment, not a court finding that CBS had manipulated the interview. PBS NewsHour’s report also described a separate context: Paramount was seeking administration approval for its proposed Skydance merger, and interview guest Brian Stelter said that was why the word “bribe” had come up in public discussion. Paramount and the FCC denied that suggestion. The reporting does not establish that merger review was exchanged for the settlement or that the administration conditioned approval on payment. This entry records the settlement and the attributed concern without treating coercion as a proven fact. Other incidents in the original card are handled separately.

children.title: Trump Signs Rescission Cutting About $1.1 Billion for Public Broadcasting
children.description_short: Trump signed a rescission bill that canceled about $1.1 billion allocated to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, according to AP reporting published by PBS.
children.description_medium: On July 24, 2025, President Donald Trump signed a bill canceling about $9 billion in previously approved foreign-aid and public-broadcasting spending. The Associated Press, published by PBS NewsHour, said about $1.1 billion was allocated to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, which finances NPR and PBS, with most of that amount distributed to more than 1,500 local stations. The bill was enacted; this report does not document later station-level effects.
children.description_long: On July 24, 2025, President Donald Trump signed a rescission bill that canceled about $9 billion in previously approved spending for public broadcasting and foreign aid. The Associated Press reported through PBS NewsHour that about $1.1 billion had been allocated to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, which financed NPR and PBS; most of that amount was distributed to more than 1,500 local public radio and television stations. The article describes a completed federal rescission, not merely a proposed cut. It says the White House had presented the bill as a test case for additional rescission packages and reports that Democrats unanimously opposed it but could not stop it. This card is limited to the signed rescission and the reported funding channel. It does not claim that the entire $1.1 billion would have gone directly to NPR or PBS, that every local station lost the same amount, or that specific station closures followed. The original record grouped this measure with separate legal disputes, media criticism, FCC inquiries, and immigration enforcement; those actions are not part of this dated entry.

children.title: White House Media Page Labels News Outlets as “Offenders”
children.description_short: By Dec. 3, 2025, a White House webpage labeled selected outlets and reports as media “offenders,” according to Reporters Without Borders.
children.description_medium: By December 3, 2025, the White House maintained a webpage labeling selected news coverage and outlets as media “offenders.” Reporters Without Borders described sections called “Media Offender of the Week,” “Hall of Shame,” and a leaderboard; it reported that CBS News, The Boston Globe, and The Independent appeared in the first section. RSF said the page offered no factual breakdown for its accusations. This entry documents the page’s existence and reported structure without adopting its accusations or RSF’s broader evaluation as established fact.
children.description_long: A Reporters Without Borders report dated December 3, 2025, described an official White House media-bias page that labeled selected outlets and reports “offenders.” It said the “Media Offender of the Week” section then named CBS News, The Boston Globe, and The Independent, and that the site also maintained a “Hall of Shame” and a leaderboard ranking outlets it alleged had reported inaccurately. RSF said the page supplied no factual breakdown for why its accusations were correct and urged the White House to remove it. This card records the existence and structure of the government page without endorsing the page’s claims or treating RSF’s criticism as a legal finding. December 3 is the date RSF described the page, not a verified launch date. The original entry grouped this page with separate settlements, appropriations, FCC investigations, and an immigration case; those incidents require their own dated sourcing and are not inferred from the webpage.

corrected_proposal.title: FBI Proffer Recorded a Witness’s Claim That Epstein Introduced Melania to Trump
corrected_proposal.description_short: A redacted former Epstein assistant told the FBI that Epstein introduced Melania and Donald Trump; the claim remains disputed.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: An FBI proffer record from 2019 was reported to contain a redacted former assistant’s statement that Jeffrey Epstein introduced Melania Trump to Donald Trump. The report says the interview occurred in July 2019 and that the document is dated November 2019. The statement is an allegation, not an established account of how the couple met; public accounts described different introductions. The record does not substantiate the original 209-file count.
corrected_proposal.description_long: In a 2019 FBI proffer, a redacted former assistant to Jeffrey Epstein said that Epstein introduced Melania Trump to Donald Trump. The Daily Beast reported that the witness made the claim during a July 2019 interview with FBI agents and federal prosecutors, and quoted the heavily redacted record as stating that Epstein introduced Melania to Donald Trump. The underlying allegation remains unverified. The article noted that the claim conflicts with Melania Trump’s memoir and with Donald Trump’s account, and reported that the Justice Department had warned that the file release could contain false or falsely submitted material. The FBI record’s November 2019 date refers to the document, while the interview was in July 2019; neither supports the frozen entry’s 2002 date. This draft therefore centers the reported contents of one proffer and omits the claim that Melania appears in 209 EFTA documents, because the supplied record cites no verifiable count for that number. It does not infer knowledge, participation, or wrongdoing from a witness statement.

children.title: Treasury Describes Read-Only Access to Fiscal Service Payment Data
children.subcategory: Federal payment systems and data access
children.description_short: Treasury said staff working with Tom Krause would have read-only access to coded Fiscal Service payment-system data.
children.description_medium: On February 4, Treasury told Congress that its staff working with Treasury employee Tom Krause would have read-only access to coded data in Bureau of the Fiscal Service payment systems. Treasury said its review had not delayed or rerouted Social Security or Medicare payments, and that agencies continued to direct their own payment processes. The source does not establish access to SSA records.
children.description_long: On February 4, 2025, Treasury sent Congress a description of its review of Bureau of the Fiscal Service payment systems. The department said Treasury staff working with Tom Krause would have read-only access to coded data in those systems. Treasury also said the review had not caused Social Security or Medicare payments to be delayed or redirected, and that the agency responsible for a payment continued to drive the process. This supports a limited account of read-only access to Treasury payment-system data. It does not establish that SSA granted DOGE access to SSA systems or that anyone accessed Social Security recipients’ files. The packet cites a Reuters report identifying the access as connected to Elon Musk’s team, but the Reuters page could not be fetched during this repair; that attribution remains unverified here. Treasury’s payment systems process federal disbursements, including Social Security and Medicare, while the records described in the second child belong to the separate Social Security Administration. Keep the agencies and events distinct.

source_fact_map.source_excerpt: Currently, Treasury staff members working with Tom Krause, a Treasury employee, will have read-only access to the coded data of the Fiscal Service’s payment systems in order to continue this operational efficiency assessment.

children.description_long: On March 24, 2025, Acting Social Security Administration Commissioner Leland Dudek filed a declaration supporting the status report required by the court’s March 20 temporary restraining order. He wrote that SSA had revoked all SSA DOGE Team 1 members’ access to systems containing personally identifiable information or systems of record. The declaration names the Enterprise Data Warehouse, Numident, Master Beneficiary Record, and Supplemental Security Record. It separately states that DOGE defendants had never had access to SSA systems of record. This evidence supports a narrow account of SSA’s access restrictions and reported compliance; it does not establish which individual previously viewed which information, whether data was copied or misused, or that the court made a final finding of unlawful access. The event is distinct from the February Treasury letter: Treasury’s Bureau of the Fiscal Service described read-only access to its payment-system data, whereas this declaration concerns SSA systems and a separate court order. The supplied February 18 date therefore does not describe either child accurately. Use March 24 for this declaration-based event and preserve the distinction between SSA DOGE Team 1 members and DOGE defendants, whom the declaration says had never accessed SSA systems of record.

children.title: Trump Orders U.S. Withdrawal from the World Health Organization
children.description_short: A Jan. 20, 2025 order directs steps toward U.S. withdrawal from WHO; it does not say membership ended that day.
children.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump issued an executive order stating that the United States intended to withdraw from the World Health Organization. It directed officials to pause future U.S. transfers, recall and reassign personnel, identify partners for necessary WHO activities, and cease negotiations on the WHO Pandemic Agreement while withdrawal was in progress. The order does not establish that membership ended on January 20.
children.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order stating that the United States intended to withdraw from the World Health Organization. It directed the Secretary of State and Office of Management and Budget to pause future U.S. funds, support and resources to WHO; recall and reassign government personnel or contractors working with the organization; and identify U.S. and international partners to assume necessary WHO activities. The order also directed the Secretary of State to cease negotiations on the WHO Pandemic Agreement and amendments to the International Health Regulations while withdrawal was in progress. This is an order to pursue withdrawal, not proof that the United States left WHO on January 20. The frozen entry incorrectly said the country withdrew from both WHO and UNESCO that day; the UNESCO action is a separate later claim and is kept in a second internal draft. The order's text does not establish the broader outcome claims in the frozen synopsis, so this card does not state that U.S. departure had already removed the country from disease-surveillance networks or produced quantified public-health harms.

corrected_proposal.title: DHS Rescinds Protected-Areas Guidance for Immigration Enforcement
corrected_proposal.description_short: Acting DHS Secretary Benjamine Huffman rescinded 2021 guidance limiting immigration enforcement in or near protected areas.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, Acting DHS Secretary Benjamine Huffman issued a memorandum rescinding the 2021 guidance for immigration enforcement in or near protected areas. DHS said the change applied to ICE and CBP and directed officers to use enforcement discretion without the prior bright-line rules. This supports a policy change, not claims that Tom Homan personally ordered raids or that specific collateral harms occurred.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On January 20, 2025, Acting Department of Homeland Security Secretary Benjamine C. Huffman issued an immediate memorandum titled “Enforcement Actions in or Near Protected Areas.” The memo superseded and rescinded the October 27, 2021 DHS guidance for Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection actions in or near areas previously designated for special protection. The memo says officers should continue using enforcement discretion and states that agency heads need not create “bright line rules” about where immigration laws may be enforced. DHS described the change as rescinding the Biden administration’s guidelines for enforcement in or near “sensitive” areas, including schools and churches. These records establish a change to department policy and expanded discretion at those locations. They do not establish that Border Czar Tom Homan personally ordered raids at churches or schools, how many such operations occurred, that families were separated as a result, or that advocates documented hundreds of collateral-harm cases. This entry is limited to the documented rescission and avoids turning a change in enforcement guidance into an unsupported account of specific raids or outcomes.

source_fact_map.source_excerpt:
January 20,2025

MEMORANDUM FOR: Caleb Vitello

Acting Director U.S.Immigration and Customs Enforcement

Pete R.Flores

Senior Official Performing the Duties of the Commissioner U.S. Customs and Border Protection

FROM: Benjamine C. Huffman Acting Secretary

SUBJECT: Enforcement Actions in or Near Protected Areas

This memorandum addresses Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) enforcement actions in or near areas that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) previously determined require special protection. It is effective immediately. This memorandum supersedes and rescinds Alejandro Mayorkas's October 27, 2021 memorandum entitled, Guidelines for Enforcement Actions in or Near Protected Areas.

source_fact_map.source_excerpt: Going forward, law enforcement officers should continue to use that discretion along with a healthy dose of common sense. It is not necessary, however, for the head of the agency to create bright line rules regarding where our immigration laws are permitted to be enforced. The Director of ICE and the Commissioner of CBP may wish to issue further guidance to assist officers in exercising appropriate enforcement discretion.

Release Date: January 21, 2025

WASHINGTON – Yesterday, Acting Department of Homeland Security Secretary Benjamine Huffman issued two directives. The first directive rescinds the Biden Administration’s guidelines for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) enforcement actions that thwart law enforcement in or near so-called “sensitive” areas.

The Trump Administration will not tie the hands of our brave law enforcement, and instead trusts them to use common sense.”

corrected_proposal.title: Trump Reinstates Schedule F as Schedule Policy/Career
corrected_proposal.description_short: Trump's January 20, 2025 executive order reinstated Schedule F under the name Schedule Policy/Career.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: On January 20, 2025, Donald Trump signed an executive order immediately reinstating the 2020 Schedule F order and renaming the category “Schedule Policy/Career.” The order directed the Office of Personnel Management to amend regulations and issue guidance on additional positions for agencies to consider. It establishes a federal workforce policy directive; it does not show how many employees were later reclassified or removed.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed “Restoring Accountability to Policy-Influencing Positions Within the Federal Workforce.” Section 2 immediately reinstated Executive Order 13957, the 2020 order creating Schedule F, subject to amendments in the new order. Those amendments replaced the excepted-service schedule label “F” with “Policy/Career” and directed the Office of Personnel Management to amend regulations that could impede implementation. The order also directed OPM to issue, within 30 days, guidance about additional position categories agencies should consider recommending for inclusion. It says employees in or applicants for these positions need not personally or politically support the President, but are required to faithfully implement administration policies; failure to do so is grounds for dismissal. These are the signed order’s rules and directions. The accessed document does not establish how many positions were later reclassified, how many employees lost protections, or whether any specific person was dismissed under it. This record describes the enacted policy mechanism, not a completed workforce purge or an asserted list of political enemies.
